title: A broadly applicable, pain-selective surgical nerve block

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a temporary, reversible nerve block that prevents pain from a surgical site while preserving movement, touch and the sense of limb position, or proprioception. It would work reliably across several procedures and anatomical regions whose pain pathways can be adequately reached. Preserving these functions is part of the intended capability; the supplied animal experiments do not establish that complete outcome in humans.

The central distinction is between stopping nerve conduction generally and selectively suppressing the signals responsible for pain. Conventional local anesthetics can also interrupt neighboring motor and nonpainful sensory signals. A pain-selective block would separate these effects sufficiently to provide surgical analgesia without the accompanying loss of useful function. The supplied research offers two different foundations: targeted drug entry into a subset of pain-sensing neurons, and an implanted system that reversibly blocks nerve conduction. Only the former provides evidence of restricted experimental pain selectivity; the implant also affects motor pathways.

significance.text: Reliable separation of surgical analgesia from motor and nonpainful sensory blockade would substantially expand regional anesthesia's capabilities. Patients could retain useful movement and sensation in the treated region while receiving effective pain control. Existing experimental work motivates this goal, but extending it to dependable surgical analgesia, preserved proprioception and many anatomical sites remains the hypothetical advance.

Conditional clinical implications: preserved limb function could support recovery, and effective local pain control could reduce the need for systemic analgesia. These benefits would need comparative clinical trials; maintaining movement alone does not establish better recovery or lower medication requirements. Preventing chronic postsurgical pain or reducing opioid use across a population would require separate evidence beyond successful short-term blockade.

The impact has practical boundaries. A block can control only pain arising through pathways it adequately reaches, so broad applicability cannot mean suitability for every operation. Pain relief also does not by itself establish unconsciousness or satisfy every anesthetic requirement of a procedure. Protective pain signaling should return after the intended treatment period: permanently eliminating warning signals would undermine the proposed benefit of a controlled, reversible intervention.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability in this proposal is the combination of sufficiently complete surgical analgesia, preservation of neighboring motor and nonpainful sensory function, predictable reversibility and applicability across multiple reachable pain pathways. The supplied studies demonstrate components of that ambition. They do not establish the full combination, and they cannot determine whether another approach had achieved it elsewhere by the review's target date of November 1, 2026.

A central scientific challenge is extending restricted selectivity into adequate coverage. The 2007 strategy used TRPV1-mediated entry of the otherwise poorly membrane-permeant sodium-channel blocker QX-314, activated in combination with capsaicin. Targeting a subset of pain-sensing neurons provides a mechanism for selectivity, but it does not establish that every pathway relevant to surgical pain is covered. A broadly useful method would have to demonstrate that its selectivity does not leave clinically important pain transmission intact.

The implanted approach illustrates a different engineering gap: reversible conduction blockade can be achieved without demonstrating pain selectivity. Its documented motor-pathway suppression means that controllable activation and recovery alone do not satisfy this concept. A device-based implementation would also need convincing evidence that activation preserves the intended motor and sensory functions while delivering adequate analgesia.

Proposed development requirements include reliable delivery to the intended pathways, consistent coverage of the operative site, controllable onset and duration, and recovery without lasting nerve dysfunction. Toxicity, tissue injury, incomplete analgesia and loss of protective sensation must be evaluated explicitly. These are requirements and potential failure modes to investigate; the supplied two-study record does not comprehensively establish their frequency or identify each as a proven present-day bottleneck across the entire field.

current_state.text: In the Nature paper published October 4, 2007, Binshtok, Bean and Woolf reported rat experiments combining QX-314 with capsaicin. The treatment reduced responses to noxious stimuli while substantially preserving motor function and tactile placing responses compared with lidocaine in their experiments. In the regional sciatic-nerve-block experiment, five of six animals had no motor deficit; one showed transient sustained flexion. This supports restricted experimental selectivity, with an observed motor-response exception, rather than universal motor sparing.

Those rat behavioral endpoints do not demonstrate surgical-level analgesia in humans or comprehensive preservation of human sensation. In particular, preserved tactile placing responses should not be expanded into a claim that touch and proprioception have both been fully preserved under clinical surgical conditions. The experiment establishes a relevant biological strategy and a limited animal result.

The author-hosted paper titled Wireless and bioresorbable triboelectric nerve block system for postoperative pain control describes an implanted, ultrasound-activated system and reversible nerve-conduction blockade in rat and porcine models. Its detailed pain-behavior experiment used a rat sciatic-nerve-crush model, with locomotion providing indirect functional evidence of pain relief. The reviewed results establish porcine conduction blockade, but do not establish porcine analgesia. The abstract's broader description of pain relief across models does not resolve that difference in experimental scope.

The implant study also reports suppression of compound muscle action potentials, demonstrating motor-pathway involvement during activation. Normal gait following implantation does not establish motor preservation while the block is active. Consequently, the device contributes evidence for reversible mixed-nerve blockade and indirect rat pain relief, rather than demonstrating the pain-selective surgical block proposed here.

The newer paper bears a 2026 copyright, but the reviewed artifact leaves its publication day blank. The research's stated online date of January 9, 2026 therefore remains unverified by the supplied review. That review had only partial extracted coverage: text from pages 21–23 was missing, and the original figures were not inspected. These limitations constrain conclusions about the complete results and safety record; they do not establish that the reported findings are false.

Neither supplied study demonstrates a broadly applicable, clinically validated pain-selective surgical block in humans. The supplied record also contains no bounded freshness-search entries, so it cannot establish the field's overall status as of November 1, 2026. The dated animal findings remain relevant evidence, while claims of current clinical availability or continued absence of the complete capability remain unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently conducted clinical trials should establish surgical-level analgesia across several procedures and anatomical sites, with prospectively measured preservation of motor function, touch and proprioception during the active block. The underlying goal of pain-restricted regional anesthesia is documented in the experimental literature; this proposed trial framework extends that goal and is not a published consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Surgical analgesia across procedures and sites preserves function during blockade

completion_criteria.text: Proposed protocol requirements: investigators should define in advance acceptable analgesia, functional preservation, block failure, rescue treatment and safety thresholds. Measurements should cover onset, the operative period, recovery and an appropriate follow-up interval. Functional testing must occur during activation, because normal function before or after treatment cannot establish selectivity while the block is working. Predictable restoration of protective pain signaling and absence of persistent neurological injury should be explicit outcomes.
completion_criteria.label: Protocols predefine thresholds for active-block selectivity and safe recovery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and clinical-value requirements: independent teams should reproduce the results, with comparative trials against appropriate existing techniques assessing patient outcomes, systemic analgesic requirements, failures and adverse effects. Any claim of low nerve-injury risk must be supported by an adequate safety dataset and follow-up rather than by the absence of injury in a small experiment. Practical evaluation should also address delivery reliability and whether the intervention can be used consistently in its intended clinical setting.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication and comparative trials establish clinical value and safety

completion_criteria.text: Proposed boundary for a completed claim: the demonstrated capability should be stated in terms of the procedures, anatomical sites, patients and treatment durations actually tested. Procedures whose relevant pain pathways cannot be adequately reached should be excluded. Even extensive successful trials would establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality; chronic-pain prevention and population opioid effects would remain separate claims unless directly evaluated.
completion_criteria.label: Capability claims remain bounded by tested clinical scope

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ANS-01, A causal theory of anesthetic-induced unconsciousness, concerns the mechanisms underlying loss of consciousness; ANS-02, A reliable real-time monitor of conscious experience during anesthesia, concerns detecting conscious experience. ANS-03 concerns selective interruption of pain transmission. Its success would neither explain unconsciousness nor establish whether a patient is conscious.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-04, Surgical unconsciousness with preserved breathing and circulatory control, shares the aim of separating a desired anesthetic effect from impairment of other functions, but targets unconsciousness and physiological control. ANS-06, Broad, active reversal of general anesthesia, shares an interest in controllable recovery, but targets reversal of general anesthesia rather than recovery from a selective peripheral block.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-05, A radically accessible, resilient anesthesia platform for essential surgery, could potentially incorporate a pain-selective block, but accessibility and resilience require separate evidence about delivery and clinical use. ANS-08, Reliable rescue oxygenation in the difficult airway, addresses airway rescue. Effective pain blockade does not itself provide oxygenation or establish rescue-airway capability.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-07, Systemic, non-opioid analgesia for severe perioperative pain, overlaps directly in the goal of controlling perioperative pain and potentially reducing systemic opioid requirements. Its intended route and coverage are systemic, whereas ANS-03 targets reachable nerves or pain pathways associated with an operative site. Either could complement the other without making them the same innovation.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-09, Mechanism-based prevention of chronic postsurgical pain, concerns persistent pain after surgery; successful acute blockade would not by itself establish prevention. ANS-10, Mechanism-guided anesthesia to prevent postoperative brain dysfunction, concerns postoperative neurological outcomes. Any benefits of ANS-03 for either outcome would require separate mechanistic and clinical evidence.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish whether the complete capability remained unmet as of November 1, 2026; no freshness-search entries were supplied.
The newer paper's exact publication date remains unverified, including the research's January 9, 2026 date.
Missing extracted text from pages 21–23 and uninspected original figures limit interpretation of the newer paper's complete results and safety evidence.
Porcine analgesia remains unestablished by the reviewed detailed results; the abstract's broader claim is not resolved by the supplied evidence.
The record does not establish clinical surgical analgesia with simultaneous preservation of motor function, touch and proprioception, nor coverage across diverse human pain pathways.
Specific clinical thresholds, suitable follow-up periods and adequate safety sample sizes remain to be defined in a future protocol.
Effects on systemic analgesic requirements, recovery, chronic postsurgical pain and population opioid use require separate comparative evidence.

brief.title: Surgical pain relief that preserves movement and touch
possible: People having surgery could have pain blocked at the operation site while keeping movement, touch and their sense of where a limb is. The effect would be temporary and reversible, and would work across several procedures and body regions whose pain pathways can be reached.
why: Patients could retain useful function while receiving local pain relief. That could support recovery and reduce the need for pain medicines that act throughout the body.

sources.who: Alexander M. Binshtok, Bruce P. Bean and Clifford J. Woolf
sources.showed: In rats, QX-314, a nerve-blocking drug, plus capsaicin, the pungent ingredient in chilli peppers, reduced pain responses while largely preserving movement and touch responses. They targeted TRPV1, a heat-sensitive channel on some pain-sensing nerve cells.
sources.quote:
Inhibition by co-applied QX-314 and capsaicin was
restricted to neurons expressing TRPV1.
sources.cited_for: Targeted drug entry can suppress some pain signals while largely sparing other nerve functions in rats.
sources.not_established: The experiments did not establish adequate surgical pain relief or full preservation of movement, touch and limb-position sense in humans.

sources.who: Young-Jun Kim, So-Hee Kim, Byung-Joon Park and collaborators
sources.showed: The team built NBAT, an implant activated by ultrasound, or high-frequency sound. It reversibly blocked nerve signals in rats and pigs, including signals to muscles. Rat movement tests gave indirect evidence of pain relief.
sources.quote:
In Fig. 2c, NBAT-implanted rats showed normal gait in terms 
of gait height and stride with the control group.
sources.cited_for: An implanted device can provide reversible nerve blocking in animals.
sources.not_established: Normal walking after implantation does not establish preserved movement during activation; pain relief in pigs was not established.

shown: Binshtok, Bean and Woolf came closest to separating pain relief from loss of function in rats, although one animal showed a temporary movement abnormality. Kim and colleagues demonstrated control over nerve blocking, but their implant also affected movement pathways. Neither study demonstrated the complete capability in humans.
missing: Human trials have yet to establish surgical pain relief alongside preserved movement, touch and limb-position sense across procedures and sites.
Reliable delivery, complete coverage of the operation site and controllable timing need demonstration.
Protective pain signals must return predictably, without lasting nerve damage or tissue injury.

milestones.label: Surgical pain relief preserves function across procedures and sites
milestones.explanation: Independent clinical trials would have to show adequate surgical pain relief with movement, touch and limb-position sense preserved during treatment. This would establish that selectivity works across procedures and body regions.

milestones.label: Protocols define successful blocking and safe recovery
milestones.explanation: Protocols would have to set advance thresholds for pain relief, function, failures, rescue treatment and safe recovery, with testing during treatment and follow-up. This would make success measurable while the block is working.

milestones.label: Independent comparisons establish clinical value and safety
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce results and compare outcomes, medicine needs, failures, harms and delivery reliability with existing care. Adequate safety follow-up would establish whether the method offers clinical value.

milestones.label: Capability claims match the clinical scope tested
milestones.explanation: Claims would have to match tested procedures, sites, patients and durations, excluding operations with unreachable pain pathways. This would define demonstrated breadth; lasting pain prevention and population opioid effects need separate evidence.

uncertain: Can targeting only some pain-sensing nerve cells block every pathway needed for adequate surgical pain relief?
What thresholds, follow-up periods and study sizes would adequately establish preserved function and safety?
Would preserved function improve recovery or reduce the need for medicines that act throughout the body?

page.title: Pain-selective regional analgesia for surgery
page.definition: A temporary regional nerve block would prevent pain from a surgical site while preserving movement, touch and the sense of joint position in the territory of the block. Protective pain sensation would return as the block wears off. The goal is for the same approach to work in distinct procedures and anatomical regions.

goal.need: In a US survey of 300 adults, 65% reported moderate to extreme pain immediately after surgery. After knee replacement, a femoral nerve block can ease pain during physical therapy while weakening the thigh muscles needed to stand and walk. Adjusting the anesthetic concentration does not reliably spare movement and position sense. A pain-selective block could let patients exercise the operated limb while it still needs pain relief, provided protective sensation returns without lasting nerve injury.

figures.caption: Postoperative pain in a US survey published online on 15 November 2013.
figures.note: Participants had undergone surgery within the preceding 5 years. These are retrospective patient reports.

statements.quote: These pharmaceuticals are highly selective, locally confined, and silence sensory neurons activated by noxious stimuli, without inhibiting neurons mediating movement or touch.
statements.context: The developer describes its proposed drugs for cough, itch, pain and inflammation.

statements.body: University Hospital Essen, Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care
statements.quote: elimination of pain transmission with a reduction in motor block and loss of proprioception
statements.context: The Neumod pilot protocol registered a comparison of local anesthetic regimens with or without electrical stimulation in patients undergoing upper- or lower-limb surgery. It specifies pain scores and analgesic use as primary outcomes and the degree of differential block as a secondary outcome.

completion.title: Controlled human studies establish reversible pain-selective surgical blockade across anatomical regions.
completion.criterion: Controlled human studies of the same regional block meet prespecified pain-control endpoints for the claimed use in distinct surgical procedures and anatomical regions. In each setting, testing in the blocked territory demonstrates preserved movement, touch and joint-position sense during analgesia and return of protective pain sensation afterwards. Postoperative analgesia and anesthesia sufficient for the operation are separate claims. Each claim is limited to the patients, sites and durations studied.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body was found to have published this combined completion test.
completion.basis: FDA's May 2026 draft treats surgical anesthesia and postoperative analgesia as distinct indications, calls for assessment of recovery and limits extrapolation between peripheral nerve blocks. The Neumod protocol assesses differential block in limb surgery. Neither specifies a common success margin for all three preserved functions during analgesia or a combined test across regions.

milestones.title: A rat nerve block reduces nociceptive responses while retaining motor score 0 and tactile placing.
milestones.criterion: After a rat sciatic block, the force required to elicit paw withdrawal with a von Frey filament and the time to withdrawal from radiant heat both increase relative to baseline. During this effect, assess gait and limb placement on the protocol's 0–2 motor scale at 15-minute intervals. Preserved function requires a score of 0 and an intact tactile placing reflex.
milestones.set_by: Binshtok, Bean and Woolf, Nature (2007), published rat sciatic-nerve protocol; these are study-specific assays, not a clinical consensus threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: Motor function of the injected leg was assessed every 15 min with a grading score of 0 (no effect; normal gait and limb placement)

milestones.title: A US investigational new drug application for a candidate block takes effect.
milestones.criterion: For a new drug requiring a US investigational new drug application (IND), pharmacology and toxicology information must support the proposed human exposure. The IND takes effect 30 days after FDA receives it unless a clinical hold intervenes, or earlier if FDA notifies the sponsor that testing may begin. Human dosing also requires compliance with informed-consent and institutional-review requirements. This is permission to investigate, not a finding of clinical efficacy.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8) and 312.40; applicable to investigational drug blocks requiring an IND.
milestones.threshold_quote: Thirty days after FDA receives the IND, unless FDA notifies the sponsor that the investigations described in the IND are subject to a clinical hold

milestones.title: Human dose and pharmacology data for a candidate drug block support the design of Phase 2 studies.
milestones.criterion: Human dosing establishes pharmacokinetics, pharmacological effects and dose-related adverse effects sufficiently to design controlled Phase 2 studies. FDA describes 20–80 participants as typical for Phase 1, not a mandatory sample size or a success threshold. The regulation does not define pain-selectivity margins.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(a), defining Phase 1 investigations of drugs.
milestones.threshold_quote: permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies.

milestones.title: Controlled studies establish preliminary efficacy of a candidate nerve block in surgical patients.
milestones.criterion: Controlled Phase 2 studies provide preliminary evidence of efficacy for a specified surgical analgesia indication and characterize common short-term risks. For prolonged-duration local analgesics, FDA's May 2026 draft recommends integrating pain scores over time and demonstrating superiority or noninferiority to the comparator throughout the proposed effect, with rescue-medication handling specified. Neither document sets a common touch or proprioception preservation cutoff.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(b), for Phase 2 drug studies. The May 2026 draft guidance gives nonbinding endpoint advice for prolonged-duration local anesthetics.
milestones.threshold_quote: evaluate the effectiveness of the drug for a particular indication

milestones.title: One surgical indication has human evidence of pain blockade, preserved function and reversal.
milestones.criterion: For one surgical procedure and anatomical region, a controlled human study meets its prespecified pain-control endpoint for the claimed intraoperative or postoperative use. Testing in the blocked territory shows preserved movement, touch and joint-position sense while pain relief is active and return of protective pain sensation after the block wears off.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback. No external protocol identified sets this combined single-indication test.

milestones.title: A candidate suppresses sodium current selectively in capsaicin-responsive rat sensory neurons.
milestones.criterion: In the published dorsal root ganglion assay, compare sodium currents before and after extracellular treatment in small capsaicin-responsive neurons and large capsaicin-insensitive neurons. Demonstrate preferential inhibition in the responsive cells against the single-agent controls.
milestones.set_by: Binshtok, Bean and Woolf, 2007 electrophysiology protocol for the QX-314 and capsaicin approach.
milestones.threshold_quote: selectively blocks sodium currents in capsaicin-responsive DRG neurons.

milestones.title: Local tolerance at the proposed block site is evaluated before first human exposure to a formulation.
milestones.criterion: Evaluate the tissues that would contact the drug formulation by the intended clinical route. Distinguish injury from the administration procedure from toxic or pharmacological effects of the formulation, and assess the significance of the findings for the proposed human exposure. If animal testing is needed, incorporate local endpoints into general toxicity studies where possible.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, guideline on non-clinical local tolerance testing, sections 1 and 4.
milestones.threshold_quote: Local tolerance should be evaluated for those sites that come into immediate contact with the medicinal product

not_found: No completed controlled human surgical study demonstrating the full combination of analgesia, preserved movement, touch and proprioception, and reversibility was located.
No consensus numerical margins for functional preservation, anatomical breadth or neurological follow-up duration were located.
No regulator or regional-anesthesia society statement questioning the feasibility or value of reversible pain-selective surgical blockade as a goal was located.

results.finding: Vocacapsaicin in bunionectomy patients (n=147): pain at rest fell 37% versus placebo over 14 days.
results.detail: The randomized, double-blind study provides preliminary efficacy evidence, but its phase is not stated and common short-term risks are not characterized. The source reports local tissue infiltration, without establishing preservation of touch or proprioception in these patients.
results.quote: During 14d after bunionectomy, vocacapsaicin 0.3 mg/mL reduced pain at rest 37% (p=0.01), ambulatory pain 30% (p=0.03), and opioid use 55% (p=0.001) vs placebo.

results.finding: Rats with sciatic nerve crush (n = 3 per group) traveled farther in the open field with ultrasound-activated NBAT (P < 0.01).
results.detail: Open-field locomotion was an indirect measure of pain-related behavior. The separate gait and rotarod tests assessed the effect of implantation.
results.quote:
NBAT group 
showed significantly enhanced locomotion (n = 3; each subject was measured 
once, mean ± s.d.).

results.finding: Rat NBAT sciatic cuff implants showed minimal local tissue reaction at 4 weeks (n = 3 reported for the H&E assessment).
results.detail: The reported sample size comes from the H&E assessment. The supplied text gives no sample size for the separate nerve and muscle staining at weeks 2 and 4.
results.quote:
show no discernible immune reactions related to implantation (week 1)  
and degradation of NBAT (week 4).

results.finding: Extracellular QX-314 plus capsaicin inhibited sodium current by 98% in 25 small capsaicin-responsive rat DRG neurons.
results.detail: The large-neuron combination result was measured after 10 minutes. The single-agent results in small neurons were measured after 5 minutes.
results.quote:
However, when QX-314 was applied together with capsaicin, the
sodium current was almost totally blocked (inhibition by 98% 6
0.4%; n 5 25) (Fig. 1a, c).

results.finding: After sciatic block with QX-314 followed by capsaicin, 5 of 6 rats retained motor score 0 and intact tactile placing.
results.detail: Mechanical and thermal effects appeared at 15 and 30 minutes, respectively, after capsaicin. The figure caption describes no motor deficit, while the results text records transient sustained flexion in one rat.
results.quote:
Five of six animals had no motor deficit (mean
motor score 0. 17 6 0.17, P 5 0.34; Fig. 4c) or a change in the placing
reflex.

results.detail: The naive-rat experiment assessed light touch by recording paw movements in response to a soft brush. The reported above-baseline von Frey result in naive rats was attributed to an earlier study.

results.finding: After outpatient laparoscopy with low-dose lidocaine–sufentanil spinal anesthesia, 80% of the 10 patients could perform deep knee bends and straight leg raises on arrival in recovery.
results.detail: The trial enrolled 30 women across three arms and included several gynecologic laparoscopic procedures. Shoulder-tip pain occurred and was treated with supplemental IV alfentanil.

results.detail: The sponsor’s protocol summarizes the animal findings without reporting group sizes, wound-model doses, or procedure-control results.

results.finding: In rabbit ulnar osteotomies (26 per group), vocacapsaicin caused no drug-related gross or microscopic findings at doses up to 0.52 mg.
results.detail: One rabbit given vocacapsaicin with ropivacaine was euthanized after persistent limited limb use and had a bent ulna at the osteotomy site. The authors could not determine whether either drug contributed.

definition = "A temporary regional nerve block would prevent pain from a surgical site while preserving movement, touch and the sense of joint position in the territory of the block. Protective pain sensation would return as the block wears off. The goal is for the same approach to work in distinct procedures and anatomical regions.". Reason: The current definition presents human demonstration across regions as an accomplished fact and leaves unclear where function must be preserved.

goal.need = "In a US survey of 300 adults, 65% reported moderate to extreme pain immediately after surgery. After knee replacement, a femoral nerve block can ease pain during physical therapy while weakening the thigh muscles needed to stand and walk. Adjusting the anesthetic concentration does not reliably spare movement and position sense. A pain-selective block could let patients exercise the operated limb while it still needs pain relief, provided protective sensation returns without lasting nerve injury.". Reason: The current rationale omits the survey result and uses rat paralysis to illustrate a functional limitation measured directly in surgical patients.

add statement by University Hospital Essen, Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, 2021: "elimination of pain transmission with a reduction in motor block and loss of proprioception". Reason: The registered perioperative protocol explicitly names preservation of motor function and position sense as objectives of selective pain blockade.

edit completion: criterion = "Controlled human studies of the same regional block meet prespecified pain-control endpoints for the claimed use in distinct surgical procedures and anatomical regions. In each setting, testing in the blocked territory demonstrates preserved movement, touch and joint-position sense during analgesia and return of protective pain sensation afterwards. Postoperative analgesia and anesthesia sufficient for the operation are separate claims. Each claim is limited to the patients, sites and durations studied."; basis = "FDA's May 2026 draft treats surgical anesthesia and postoperative analgesia as distinct indications, calls for assessment of recovery and limits extrapolation between peripheral nerve blocks. The Neumod protocol assesses differential block in limb surgery. Neither specifies a common success margin for all three preserved functions during analgesia or a combined test across regions."; refs = [2, 4, 5, 13]. Reason: The wording should distinguish pain relief after surgery from anesthesia sufficient for the operation and explain which part of the test FDA addresses.

add milestone after None: "A candidate suppresses sodium current selectively in capsaicin-responsive rat sensory neurons.". Reason: The isolated-neuron experiment establishes selectivity at the cellular level before the whole-animal block tests behavior.

edit m1: criterion = "After a rat sciatic block, the force required to elicit paw withdrawal with a von Frey filament and the time to withdrawal from radiant heat both increase relative to baseline. During this effect, assess gait and limb placement on the protocol's 0\u20132 motor scale at 15-minute intervals. Preserved function requires a score of 0 and an intact tactile placing reflex."; threshold_quote = "Motor function of the injected leg was assessed every 15 min with a grading score of 0 (no effect; normal gait and limb placement)"; threshold_ref = 2; refs = [2]. Reason: The current criterion mixes two published results with the rat assay and obscures the distinction between a placing reflex and a human sensory report.

add milestone after m1: "Local tolerance at the proposed block site is evaluated before first human exposure to a formulation.". Reason: Delayed hypersensitivity and nerve injury after an initially effective rat block show why local tolerance needs a separate assessment before human exposure.

edit m2: title = "A US investigational new drug application for a candidate block takes effect."; threshold_quote = "Thirty days after FDA receives the IND, unless FDA notifies the sponsor that the investigations described in the IND are subject to a clinical hold"; threshold_ref = 8. Reason: The title implies that every candidate needs express FDA permission, although a US drug investigation can proceed when its required IND takes effect.

edit m3: title = "Human dose and pharmacology data for a candidate drug block support the design of Phase 2 studies."; threshold_quote = "permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies."; threshold_ref = 9. Reason: The existing quotation marks the start of human dosing, whereas the milestone requires enough human pharmacology data to design Phase 2.

edit m4: set_by = "FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(b), for Phase 2 drug studies. The May 2026 draft guidance gives nonbinding endpoint advice for prolonged-duration local anesthetics."; threshold_quote = "evaluate the effectiveness of the drug for a particular indication"; threshold_ref = 9. Reason: The current quotation describes entry into Phase 3, while subsection (b) directly defines the indication-specific Phase 2 evaluation.

edit m5: criterion = "For one surgical procedure and anatomical region, a controlled human study meets its prespecified pain-control endpoint for the claimed intraoperative or postoperative use. Testing in the blocked territory shows preserved movement, touch and joint-position sense while pain relief is active and return of protective pain sensation after the block wears off."; set_by = "Atlas fallback. No external protocol identified sets this combined single-indication test."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; refs = [2, 4, 5, 13]. Reason: The single-indication test needs to identify the intended period of pain control and require sensory and motor assessment in the territory receiving analgesia.
